entries.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model amid safety concerns
entries.summary: The decision comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful and autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up.
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

The decision comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful and autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up.

Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has abandoned plans to release a next-generation AI model after internal testing found that the system failed to meet the company's safety and alignment standards.

GPT-6.1 Astra, which is designed to handle increasingly complex tasks with less human intervention, had been scheduled to debut in October but tests reportedly found that the model displayed higher levels of deceptive behavior than its predecessors.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said the model had improved in some areas but had not met the company's standards for staying within authorized boundaries or clearly communicating its actions to users.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users," Jain said. "But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms ⁠of safety and ​alignment."

Pressure builds for stronger AI oversight

The postponement comes as OpenAI and other AI companies face growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly powerful and autonomous models.

Some of these models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic have been involved in security incidents during testing.

Earlier this month, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei joined other industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.

Leading AI executives are set to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday to discuss the need for finding a balance between AI innovation and oversight.

OpenAI pledges to rebuild trust after government website hack

On Tuesday, OpenAI admitted that its models had even accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorization as part of internal training and evaluation exercises in June.

The company said ‌the activity ‌involved ​websites and systems linked to Services Australia, ​the NSW Bureau of ⁠Crime ​Statistics and Research, ​the Victorian ​Department of ‌Health and the Australian ​Institute ⁠of Health and ⁠Welfare.

The incursion, which occurred in June, was not made public until last week.

In a blog post, the ChatGPT maker apologized for the hacking and acknowledged it ‌mishandled its response ⁠and ⁠pledged to take accountability to "rebuild trust with the Australian people."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: France: Student protests over conditions at French high schools fuel political clashes
entries.summary: Over 160 people were arrested and dozens injured after student protests in France descended into violence. With a presidential election approaching, senior politicians are pointing fingers at each other.
entries.content:
France

France: Student protests fuel political clashes

September 29, 2026

Over 160 people were arrested and dozens injured after student protests in France descended into violence. With a presidential election approaching, senior politicians are pointing fingers at each other.

Student protests spread to high schools across France on Monday, resulting in dozens of injuries, over 160 arrests and arguments between senior politicians — a day ahead of a nationwide strike by public sector workers and seven months ahead of the presidential election.

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week in protest at overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor quality learning materials and teacher shortages.

The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regions including Lille in the north, Marseille in the south and Sedan in the east.

Video footage on French media showed student protesters lighting flares and firing fireworks, even inside a school building, while police officers responded with tear gas.

French student protests: what have politicians said?

As of Monday night, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported incidents at around 180 establishments resulting in 164 arrests and injuries to 12 students, three teachers and 12 police officers.

He acknowledged that the "difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed" but said: "This wasn't about making demands, it was really violence in its purest form."

He added that "a number of individuals … were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes and projectiles [and] clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces."

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the "escalation" of the situation "irresponsible" and said: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."

'Hands off our youth!' French politicians clash over protests

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that the protests, which he described as a "classic high school student movement," were being exploited by violent elements — and took aim at the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon.

"There is a political hijacking of the blockades by elected officials from France Unbowed," he said.

Earlier on Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."

"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."

In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, the LFI-run local council called the students' demands "legitimate" and published a statement reading:

"Let [the authorities] come and talk to [the students] and see for themselves whether the youth are being instrumentalized, or whether they are simply capable of thinking, organizing themselves and defending their own study conditions and their future."

France: strikes — and an election — to come

The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the French union that defends the interests of high school students, said it would urge a nationwide blockade of schools on Tuesday — coinciding with planned strike action by public sector workers.

French primary school teachers' unions said they expected some 40% of teachers to be off work on Tuesday.

With a key presidential election only seven months away and incumbent President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from standing for a third term, French politicians from across the ideological spectrum are seeking issues that resonate with voters.

Melenchon, a 75-year-old veteran anti-capitalist who finished third in the 2022 presidential election, is popular among younger, left-leaning voters.

His LFI party was one of the left-wing outfits which joined the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front or NFP) coalition in 2024 to oppose the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN) in legislative elections.

The coalition beat the RN but the elections produced a divided parliament which has been dogged by political deadlock and votes of no-confidence.

Prime Minister Lecornu is still trying to build enough support to pass a 2027 state budget, but his government is besieged by opponents who are unwilling to accept spending cuts while energy costs continue to rise.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Israel's Netanyahu holds secret meeting with UAE president
entries.summary: After confirming a rare meeting, Netanyahu's office has denied suggestions that the Israeli prime minister requested that Abu Dhabi deny reports that it had warned Israel about an impending Hamas attack in 2023.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel's Netanyahu holds secret meeting with UAE president

September 29, 2026

After confirming a rare meeting, Netanyahu's office has denied suggestions that the Israeli prime minister requested that Abu Dhabi deny reports that it had warned Israel about an impending Hamas attack in 2023.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly met with the president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, both governments confirmed late on Monday.

"The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them," read an Emirati statement.

Netanyahu's office said the visit "focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges."

The secret trip came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the UAE president had warned Netanyahu about an imminent threat from the Palestinian militant group Hamas ahead of the deadly attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 — a warning which the Israeli premier allegedly failed to pass on to security services.

Indeed, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Monday that the purpose of Netanyahu's visit had been to request that Sheikh Mohamed deny having given such a warning.

Netanyahu's office denied that the prime minister had made any such request, just as it had also denied the original report.

Netanyahu files complaint against Israeli broadcaster

Earlier on Monday, before the confirmation of Netanyahu's trip, Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet filed a complaint against Channel 12, accusing it of violating censorship rules by reporting the visit before the prime minister had returned to Israel.

"This evening, Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation," read a statement from Netanyahu's office.

It noted that the report had been made public while the premier's plane was still outside Israeli airspace and therefore "endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad" spy agency and other top security officials.

Israel and the UAE: diplomatic relations

Sheikh Mohamed's hosting of Netanyahu was a significant development at a time when the Israeli leader is seen by many across the Middle East as the chief propagator of the war in Gaza, which has seen over 70,000 Palestinians killed — many of them civilians.

It is also the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leaders after denying reports of a previous Netanyahu trip in May.

The UAE is one of only a handful of Arab nations which maintain official diplomatic ties with Israel after signing the Abraham Accords during US President Donald Trump's first term in 2020.

The UAE condemned the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 as a "serious and grave escalation" and said it was "appalled" by reports of Israeli citizens being taken hostage.

But relations have also been strained by Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, with the UAE denouncing "ongoing Israeli violations" in the Palestinian enclave.

Nevertheless, Israel reportedly deployed Iron Dome air defense systems, together with personnel to operate them, to the UAE during the war against Iran, as the Gulf state faced retaliatory attacks from Tehran.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
entries.summary: The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.
entries.content:
September 29, 2026

The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.

US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo. 

Earlier in September as part of "operation economic outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and potentially lose access to the US financial system. 

The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies. 

For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.

Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.

For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.

The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.

For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.

Major Middle East routes canceled

Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously for safety reasons that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia have been seriously disrupted.

On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.

Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.

A passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.

As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.

Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.

The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.

More travelers use land crossings

With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.

One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.

"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.

For families, older people, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.

Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.

That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.

Iran's shaky aviation industry

Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions. 

Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.

An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.

When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.

Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.

"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.

"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.

Iran isolated by air and sea

Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.

Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.

If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.

The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult. 

If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states. 

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Iranian human rights lawyer Nasrin Sotoudeh wins the 2026 Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize
entries.summary: The Council of Europe awarded human rights lawyer Nasrin Sotoudeh with the Vaclav Havel human rights prize. She is a prominent advocate for the rights of women, children and political prisoners.
entries.content:
September 28, 2026

The Council of Europe awarded human rights lawyer Nasrin Sotoudeh with the Vaclav Havel human rights prize. She is a prominent advocate for the rights of women, children and political prisoners.

Human rights lawyer Nasrin Sotoudeh is one of Iran's best-known human rights activists. On September 28, she was awarded the Council of Europe's Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize.

In 2026, Sotoudeh was one of three finalists for prize. The other nominees were the Iranian-American journalist and women's rights activist Masih Alinejad and the Hungarian human rights lawyer Marta Pardavi.

The Council of Europe is honoring Sotoudeh's longstanding commitment to human rights and her work, which she has carried out at considerable personal risk.

The council said Sotoudeh campaigned against compulsory hijab laws and the death penalty, "despite repeated arrests, lengthy imprisonment and great personal risk."

Who is Nasrin Sotoudeh?

Human rights lawyer Sotoudeh is committed to women's rights, the rights of political prisoners, and the abolition of the death penalty. She has represented numerous activists, journalists, members of religious minorities, and people sentenced to death.

"In moments like this, we remember past struggles, we recall our shared ideals and we think of the individuals across the globe who stand with us," Sotoudeh in a video statement from Tehran.

As early as 2012, she was awarded the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize, along with film director Jafar Panahi. At the time, she was in prison and was unable to accept the award in person.

In 2019, she had been sentenced to 33 years in prison and 148 lashes. One reason for the sentence was her work as a lawyer for women who had protested against Iran's headscarf mandate.

Even while in prison, she continued her advocacy for human rights. In 2020, Sotoudeh went on a hunger strike at Evin Prison to protest the conditions of detention and the situation of political prisoners. That same year, she was among the recipients of the Alternative Nobel Prize (Right Livelihood Award) and learned of the award while in prison.

Voice for women's rights in Iran

During Iran's nationwide "Woman, Life, Freedom" protest movement in 2022, Sotoudeh once again became a leading voice for the rights of Iranian women.

Her decades-long commitment symbolizes the enduring resistance against state restrictions and repression. She has been arrested repeatedly and sentenced to long prison terms, including in April 2026. In May, she was released on bail.

The Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize recognizes "outstanding civil society action in defense of human rights" in Europe and elsewhere. The prize is worth €60,000 and is awarded by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) in cooperation with the Charter 77 Foundation.

This article was translated from German

entries.title: Sicily: Mount Etna ash disrupts Catania flights again
entries.summary: A thick ash cloud from Mount Etna has been disrupting flights to Catania in Sicily for several days. Italy and Europe's most active volcano, Etna has impacted air travel several times this summer.
entries.content:
Italy

Sicily: Mount Etna ash disrupts Catania flights again

September 28, 2026

A thick ash cloud from Mount Etna has been disrupting flights to Catania in Sicily for several days. Italy and Europe's most active volcano, Etna has impacted air travel several times this summer.

Flight restrictions at Italy's Catania Aiport were extended on Monday, following disruptions to services over the weekend. 

A thick ash cloud emanating from the nearby Mount Etna volcano has prompted authorities to halt flights. 

What do we know about the disruption?

The Sicilian aiport's operator, SAC, said that all flight operations at the hub had been suspended until at least midnight local time (2200 GMT/UTC) on Monday night.

It said that where possible arrivals and departures were transferring to Sicily's other airports in Palermo and Comiso. Catania is Italy's fifth-busiest airport, and Sicily's largest hub.

SAC advised passengers to check the status of their flights prior to setting off for the airport.

The Mediterranean island is a popular holiday destination but travelers have faced frequent disruptions this summer because of eruptions and more commonly because of ash emanating from Etna. 

Ash from the northeast crater of the mountain is being carried southward by the wind.

Italian Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV) said the ash did not appear to indicate an imminent explosive phase.

What is Mount Etna?

Mount Etna is a roughly 3,400 meter (roughly 11,100 feet) stratovolcano on Sicily's eastern coast. Its precise height is ever changing, particularly amid periods of high activity when it can shed a few meters.

The city of Catania is located not far to the south.

Etna is one of the tallest active volcanoes in Europe and Italy's highest peak south of the Alps.

It's in an almost constant state of low-level activity and erupts in a more pronounced manner fairly frequently. It has caused disruptions at Catania airport several times this year, and in recent years. 

A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the first volcanic activity took place at Etna about half a million years ago.

Both Roman and Greek mythology asserted that the god of blacksmithing — either Vulcan or Hephaestus — had his forge beneath Mount Etna.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: SpaceX launches supersized Starship into orbit
entries.summary: Starship is the biggest and most powerful spacecraft ever built and it is meant to support NASA's Artemis moon program.
entries.content:
September 28, 2026

Starship is the biggest and most powerful spacecraft ever built and it is meant to support NASA's Artemis moon program.

US airspace giant SpaceX on Monday launched its Starship spacecraft into orbit. The firm hoped the Starship could complete six full laps around Earth in order to prove its readiness for NASA's Artemis moon program.

"Starship is orbital," Mission Control announced to cheers. The Launch took place at Starbase, Texas. The laps were supposed to last around 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile.

But just an hour after liftoff, SpaceX said it planned to bring Starship back to Earth after about three hours in orbit, cutting the 10-hour trip short.

Starship launches 26 satellites

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praised SpaceX for reaching orbit and "managing every step in a safe, responsible and especially inspirational way."

Starship is the biggest and most powerful spacecraft ever built, it was propelled by a 407-foot (124-meter) rocket that was designed from the start to be fully reusable.

The spacecraft was loaded with 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites, which were released one by one, to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service.

"All 26 Starlink V3 operational satellites deployed and operating nominally," SpaceX CEO ElonMusk wrote on X.

SpaceX's so-called V3 satellites are designed to unfold their antennas and solar panels after release before establishing connections with Earth and other Starlink satellites.

SpaceX began flying Starship in 2023 and the program has seen its successes and failures of successive tests. Technical challenges remain before Starship can fulfill its mandates, such as conduct commercial flights, deploy data centers in orbit or reach the Moon or the Red Planet.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
entries.summary: Deniz Goktas was convicted of two of three charges, including "insulting" the president, but was released pending the appeal process. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.
entries.content:
Turkey

Turkey: Comedian convicted for 'insulting' Erdogan in show

September 28, 2026

Deniz Goktas was convicted of two of three charges, including "insulting" the president, but was released pending the appeal process. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.

A Turkish comedian was convicted in Istanbul on Monday on charges of "insulting" President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and "insulting religious values" during a stand-up performance in June. 

The judge provisionally sentenced Deniz Goktas to 19 months in prison, but ordered his release pending the judicial review and appeal process that would finalized the verdict.

It was not immediately clear how long this process might take.

NATO member and EU aspirant Turkey routinely tries people on speech-related offenses, particularly and famously when it comes to supposed "insults" of its longserving leader Erdogan.

What was the case about?

Deniz Goktas, 32, was arrested on July 3, a week after releasing a YouTube video of his show that was watched nearly 9 million times and a few days after shorter clips he posted on X enjoyed similar rapid success. 

He faced an array of charges related to content in his "Dead Sea" show. Goktas referred to his impending court appointment online on Sunday, in one of his irreverent social media posts from his cell.

Goktas was accused of insulting Erdogan, of inciting public hatred and hostility — via jokes about Islam — and of praising crime and criminals, an additional charge added by prosecutors tied to a joke about an organized crime family, the Daltons

His trial is the latest in a widening crackdown on people seen as critical of Turkey's moderate Islamist government. Hundreds of politicians, artists, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists are among those to face detention or trial. 

What did Goktas say in his defense in court?

Goktas did not dispute the content from his popular show, but did argue in court that he had committed no crimes with his jokes.

Prosecutors had for instance singled out a pair of references he made to President Erdogan as a "dictator" as illegal insults.

"Dictator is not an insult: it is a political characterization," Goktas told the court. "As the president and leader of the party that has ruled the country for 25 years, a political comedy show in which Erdogan's name is never mentioned would be neither sincere nor have any connection to reality."

He said that Erdogan should be "open to the art of satire," as he said past presidents in Turkish democracy were.

"The joke hasn't changed. What has changed is the increasingly fragile leadership that can no longer tolerate the joke," he said.

The judge nevertheless convicted Gotkas of insulting Erdogan, and downgraded the charge he faced of "inciting hatred and hostility" with jokes about Islam, instead convicting him of the lesser supposed crime of "insulting religious values."

He cleared the comedian of the third charge of allegedly praising criminality.

Goktas has spent just under three months in pretrial detention, which should count as time served in any potential custodial sentence.

Erdogan the only claimant, Diyanet religious authority among those to complain

According to the Turkish NGO the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA), prosecutors cited more than 500 applications to prosecute the performer regarding the show. 

They were issued to the Presidential Communication Center that monitors such issues. One of the groups to provide a tipoff was the government-sponsored Presidency of Religious affairs, better known as Diyanet.

Erdogan, in charge of Turkey either as prime minister or later president since 2003, was named as the sole complainant.

His government has attracted attention in recent years for its prosecution of people deemed to have unfairly criticized the authorities, and for the various lawsuits against leading members of the opposition, particularly the CHP. The Turkish president's litigious streak also became headline news in Germany around a decade ago, when he pursued star TV comedian Jan Böhmermann.

Meanwhile the MLSA said that Goktas' jokes alleged to have the potential to "publicly incite hatred and hostility" took aim at fundamentalist Islam, including a reference to women in full-coverage swimsuits being "divers" and joking about "suicide bombers who fast."

Turkey nominally has a secular constitution and guarantees of free speech. However, the EU and the US have often criticized its application of these standards.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom wrote in a 2022 report that Erdogan's government increasingly relied on speech-based prosecution to "silence individuals who express criticism in religious terms, disclose beliefs or a lack thereof that differ from those of the majority of the population, or engage with religion in a way perceived as 'mocking' or 'irreverent.'"

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: What do Manchester City's charges mean for German football?
entries.summary: Manchester City have reportedly been found guilty of major financial rule breaches. What does this mean for German football?
entries.content:
September 28, 2026

Manchester City have reportedly been found guilty of major financial rule breaches. What does this mean for German football?

What has happened to Manchester City?

Manchester City have reportedly been found guilty on 114 of the 115 Premier League charges over alleged breaches of financial regulations. They relate to a period between 2009 to 2018 and include allegations around financial reporting, disclosure of player and manager payments, compliance with UEFA and Premier League financial rules, and cooperation with the investigation. The Premier League has yet to comment, with the news having first been reported by The Athletic.

The process started when the charges were brought in February 2023. The review was started in 2024 before the reported verdict of guilty on almost all charges arrived on September 25, 2026.

The English champions, owned in practice by the United Arab Emirates' ruling family, deny all charges and insist their case is supported by a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence."

Has this happened before?

The Premier League has long had a reputation for rampant capitalism, but it has started to enforce financial regulations that control spending in recent years.

In 2026, Chelsea were fined €11.6 million ($13.8 million) and given a suspended ban from registering new players for two transfer windows for breaching rules relating to payments to agents between 2009 and 2022. The club did avoid a six-point deduction though. In the recent years before, Everton and Nottingham Forest were docked Premier League points for breaking profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

City previously won, for the most part, a similar battle with UEFA. The 2023 UEFA Champions League winners were hit with a huge fine by UEFA in 2014 over a breach of the organization's FFP (Financial Fair Play) rules. Then, in February 2020, UEFA handed City a €30-million fine and banned the club from competing in the Champions League for two years for falsely inflating sponsorship revenues between 2012 and 2016. But in July of the same year, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned the ban and reduced the fine to €10 million. City denied all charges and did not miss a game in Europe's premier club competition.

The key difference in City's current case to Chelsea's earlier in the year is that Chelsea self-reported and admitted guilt, which allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League over the sanction. City have stressed that they are innocent throughout.

Has something like this happened in Germany before?

German football is by no means immune to scandals or corruption. The most prominent examples are the 1971 match-fixing scandal in which players took bribes to throw matches, and the 2005 match-fixing scandal involving referee Robert Hoyzer, who confessed to fixing and betting on matches in the second division and German Cup.

The majority of financial breaches have come from clubs not being able to prove they were financially viable. Both 1860 Munich and Uerdingen are examples of this, but major systematic abuses or breaches have not happened because the structure of German football is designed to prevent it.

Why is something like this not possible in Germany?

Mainly because of the 50+1 rule. In place since 1999, the rule stipulates that the parent club, for example Bayern Munich, must hold at least 50% plus one vote in its spun-off professional football company – in this case, FC Bayern München Fußball AG. This ensures that the majority of voting rights always lie with the club and its members.

The rule prevents external investors from taking complete control of a club and managing it solely according to financial criteria. It is also meant to ensure a certain level of equality, as it is not possible for a club to invest disproportionately more money than other clubs thanks to its powerful investor with a controlling stake.

The vast majority of organized fans in Germany oppose the commercialization of football. The 50+1 rule makes many fans in Germany not just paying spectators but active club members who can, for example, have a say inimportant club decisions.

Critics argue that the rule puts German football clubs at a financial disadvantage. Spending in the Premier League proves that to be true, but City's reported offenses are also proof of why the league's sustainable structure matters. The Bundesliga has been approached by DW for comment.

Do these charges have an impact in Germany?

Not until the ruling and punishment are final. However, one of the main talking points is what City's success prevented other teams from claiming, whether it be prize money, Champions League places or transfer opportunities. These are compensatory claims that might be explored should the charges remain after appeals.

What happens next?

Manchester City face possible points deductions, expulsion, financial penalties or the stripping of their titles. It is unclear when the decision on what the punishment will be will come, especially given that City are expected to appeal.

The outcome also has significant impacts for the Premier League. In taking on one of its biggest clubs, having successfully punished two smaller ones, they risk appearing toothless. Certainly the eyes of European football will be on them as the impact of the decision will put the integrity of the competition into focus.

It may also see more English fans call for a model like the 50+1 rule to be integrated. Some voices were raised in England after the Saudi sovereign wealth fund PIF took over Premier League club Newcastle United in 2021, and others continued during the attempted establishment of a European Super League in 2021.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Why the latest action from India's youth-led 'cockroach' movement is targeting the election chief
entries.summary: The 'cockroach' movement has emerged as an influential force in Indian politics. Its latest campaign targets the election commission amid a wider debate over voter rolls and public trust in electoral institutions.
entries.content:
India

Why India's cockroach movement wants the election chief out

September 28, 2026

The 'cockroach' movement has emerged as an influential force in Indian politics. Its latest campaign targets the election commission amid a wider debate over voter rolls and public trust in electoral institutions.

India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties have demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision.

According to the probe, published in The Indian Express newspaper, some key decisions linked to the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls that began last year were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.

The Indian Express said that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data.

In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission of India (ECI) acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The allegations presented "only one part of the picture," and "differing views" were a routine "part of decision-making," the ECI said in a statement cited by local media.

'Cockroach' movement founder calls for demonstrations

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke called Kumar "the biggest threat to India's democracy" and demanded his resignation.

Dipke threatened to launch nationwide protests, beginning in Mumbai on October 2, the birthday of India's founding father Mahatma Gandhi, if Kumar did not quit by Saturday.

The Saturday deadline passed without Kumar stepping down.

After Mumbai police denied permission for the planned October 2 protest, Dipke posted on X calling on supporters to submit to mass arrests rather than comply with the ban.

Supporters staged protests on Friday and pledged to continue mobilizing despite the restrictions.

Opposition parties echoed the CJP's criticism of Kumar and the Election Commission.

Pawan Khera of the main opposition Congress party said that "Gyanesh Kumar has done nothing short of treason."

"If decisions relating to the SIR were taken without the knowledge or approval of two of the three election commissioners... then those decisions and the entire SIR exercise are legally invalid," Khera said on social media.

Congress and other opposition parties have accused the ECI of colluding with India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to manipulate voter lists and win state elections in recent years, charges both the commission and the BJP have denied.

What are the demands of India's CJP movement?

The 'Cockroach' movement, which has millions of followers on social media, forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July following widespread student-led street protests. 

The group has laid out three demands: Kumar's resignation and criminal proceedings against him, a freeze on the SIR and the suspension of all upcoming elections, and the repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of the election commissioners of India.

Civil rights activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's decision to target the poll panel reflects wider concerns over the lack of transparency surrounding the SIR.

"There is an absence of public consultation or a clear explanation for launching the exercise, as well as the findings of the newspaper that the two election commissioners had raised repeated objections to key decisions," Johri told DW.

"Restoring public confidence will require Kumar's removal, stopping the SIR and an independent review of the millions of names excluded from the draft rolls."

From education protests to electoral politics

Political activist Sudheendra Kulkarni sees the CJP's latest campaign as that of a pressure group rather than an emerging standalone political force.

"I do not see any separate political future for the CJP. It may remain as a pressure group for some time. But as the next parliamentary election approaches, it will have to align itself with the opposition alliance," Kulkarni told DW.

Others see greater weight in the CJP's shift.

Political analyst and commentator Radhika Ramaseshan said the CJP widening its focus will not weaken what it started.

"I don't think if the CJP enlarged the ambit of its concerns and built protests around [them], it would take away from the salience and power of the first issue it highlighted," Ramaseshan told DW. "Voter rights and enfranchisement is fundamental to a citizen's existence, to upholding the sanctity of the Indian constitution."

"These are not abstractions or procedural matters. They impinge on the lives of first-time voters who make up the bulk of the CJP," she added.

What happens now?

With Kumar refusing to resign, attention will now turn to the CJP's promise of street protests starting in Mumbai on October 2.

But a protest group alone cannot simply remove a CEC. Under India's constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a process requiring action by both houses of Parliament and a special majority, on grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity.

"The CJP's significance would be in increasing pressure and forcing scrutiny of the ECI's functioning," former Chief Election Commissioner S Y Quraishi's told DW.

He argues that the reported unilateral decisions are the more serious issue and should be subjected to an independent legal and technical audit.

"The practical route is judicial scrutiny, not street removal. The decisions taken unilaterally by the CEC in a three-member commission could be challenged as invalid, with the Supreme Court potentially needed to intervene," he said.

"Where the commission will not act, the Supreme Court will have to step in," added Quraishi.

The CJP's latest campaign puts it directly into one of India's most contentious disputes over electoral administration.

Whether it can sustain that momentum against the Election Commission will be a very different test for a movement that is still trying to define its place in Indian politics.

Edited by: Keith Walker
